tier_reason: The README Performance table compares crc32fast 1.0.0 (baseline and pclmulqdq variants) with the `crc` crate 1.8.1 in ns/iter and MB/s. It gives no CPU model, compiler or flags, and the current criterion harness (benches/bench.rs) no longer benchmarks the `crc` crate, so these are first-party numbers without methodology: tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table: `crc` crate 1.8.1 at 4,926 ns/iter (207 MB/s); crc32fast 1.0.0 baseline at 683 ns/iter (1,499 MB/s); crc32fast pclmulqdq at 140 ns/iter (7,314 MB/s). That is about 7.2x and 35x over `crc` (derived from page data).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 338 stars; about 712M all-time crates.io downloads and 1,296 reverse dependencies; flate2 1.1.10 and png 0.18.1 both depend on crc32fast ^1.2.0 (crates.io)
corrections.caveats: The README benchmark table gives no CPU model or compiler flags. It is historical: it compares crc32fast 1.0.0 against `crc` 1.8.1, both 2018-era versions, and does not cover the newer vpclmulqdq AVX2/AVX-512 and aarch64 3-way paths. The current criterion benchmark (benches/bench.rs) measures only crc32fast itself, so nothing in the repo can reproduce the comparison. The GitHub license API reports only Apache-2.0, but Cargo.toml and the README declare MIT OR Apache-2.0, and both LICENSE files are present.

notes: The numbers, license, stars and last commit (2026-09-21, 'Centralize state handling') all match. The baseline here is the Rust `crc` crate, not zlib. Adoption is very high (flate2 and png depend on it).

tier_reason: The README gives only ratios: about 12.5x decode and 11.5x encode over the library's own scalar LUT codec, plus Node.js module ratios. The Node benchmark scripts (benchmark/hex-decode.js, benchmark/hex-encode.js) are public, but there is no C++ harness and no CPU model, compiler or raw throughput, so these are first-party numbers without methodology: tier C.

corrections.workload: AVX2 hex decode/encode of byte buffers. The C++ ratios are against the library's own scalar look-up-table codec (decodeHexLUT/encodeHex in src/hex.cc). The Node.js ratios come from benchmark/hex-*.js. There, the encode baseline is Node's built-in Buffer#toString('hex'), but the decode baseline labelled 'node' is the addon's own scalar decodeHexLUT, not Buffer.from(str, 'hex').
corrections.claimed_speedup: C++: decoding about 12.5x and encoding about 11.5x over scalar. Node.js module: about 2.12x faster decoding for short string inputs (< 1,031,913 chars), about 12x faster decoding for some long strings, Buffers and TypedArrays, and about 5.5x faster encoding. The README does not name the Node.js baseline.
corrections.caveats: The README gives ratios only: no CPU model, compiler version or raw throughput, so tier C is the cap. The README does not say what the Node.js figures are measured against. In the current scripts the decode 'node' baseline is the addon's own scalar LUT, and the decode script still references decodeHexBMI, which is no longer exported. The encode script's input buffer is all zeros because its fill loop discards Math.random(). There is no C++ benchmark harness; Book1.xlsx holds only hand-computed cycle and port estimates. The library does not validate input and needs AVX2. The last code change was 2022-09-19; the only 2026 commit (2026-01-22) is a Dependabot lodash bump in /benchmark.

notes: The numbers match the README. Only the baseline attribution needed fixing: the decode ratios are not demonstrably against Node's built-in hex decoder. 'Active' status is correct under the 12-month rule, but it rests on a Dependabot-only commit, so real maintenance is closer to stale.

tier_reason: The paper DOI returns 403 (bot check) through both curl and WebFetch; its Crossref abstract says only 'multiply', gives no numbers, and it is an unreviewed Authorea preprint. The simdutf README fastbase64 Performance section does give first-party numbers against the system base64 tool, with CPU models and a public script (scripts/base64bench.sh), but no compiler or flags, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README fastbase64 table (median wall-clock ms from scripts/base64bench.sh, decoding 100 MB of random data): Apple M4 Max 1433.5 ms for the system base64 vs 52.7 ms for fastbase64 (about 27x), and Xeon Gold 6548N on Linux 291.8 ms vs 84.4 ms (about 3.5x) (derived from page data). At 1 MB the two are near parity. The Lemire 2025 preprint abstract says only that the new functions 'multiply the base64 decoding speed compared to traditional methods', with no factor given.
corrections.workload: Command-line base64 decoding (and encoding) of 1, 10 and 100 MB random files with simdutf's fastbase64 tool, which uses simdutf's forgiving-base64 decoder, against the OS base64 utility (GNU coreutils on Linux, BSD/macOS base64 otherwise). The ignorable-character SIMD algorithm itself is described in Lemire's Authorea preprint (DOI 10.22541/au.175692137.72576748/v1).
corrections.hardware: Apple M4 Max; Intel Xeon Gold 6548N (Linux)
corrections.caveats: The Authorea preprint 'Base64 Decoding with Ignorable Characters using SIMD instructions' (Lemire, 2025; DOI 10.22541/au.175692137.72576748/v1, with an earlier v1 at 10.22541/au.173866897.72952916/v1) is not peer-reviewed and its full text is behind a bot check. It is not on arXiv or HAL, so none of its numbers were verified. The replacement numbers are end-to-end CLI timings that include process startup and I/O, with no compiler or flags stated. On Linux the decode comparison is not like-for-like: GNU base64 decodes its own 76-column line-wrapped output while fastbase64 decodes its own unwrapped output. The repo is dual-licensed Apache-2.0 or MIT; the code under benchmarks/competition is 'for research purposes only' and is not part of the library.

notes: The paper could not be fetched (Authorea 403 through curl and WebFetch), so I replaced benchmark_url with the README fastbase64 Performance section, which has verifiable numbers and CPU models; the tier stays C. simdutf appears in known_list.txt only because wave 7 merged it, so it is not a pre-existing duplicate. The license is dual (Apache-2.0 OR MIT), not Apache-2.0 alone.
